sources.title: GOLD: 2026 COPD Report and Pocket Guide

questions.question: A patient has episodic wheeze and chest tightness that worsen at night and with exercise. Baseline spirometry is normal on an asymptomatic day. Which next diagnostic principle is most appropriate?
choices: Seek objective evidence of variable expiratory airflow limitation rather than excluding asthma from one normal test
Diagnose COPD because all episodic wheeze is fixed obstruction
Exclude respiratory disease permanently because FEV1 is normal once
Use chest radiography alone to confirm airway hyperresponsiveness
rationales: Asthma symptoms and airflow limitation vary; repeat spirometry during symptoms, bronchodilator response, peak-flow variability, or other appropriate testing may document variability.
COPD is characterized by persistent obstruction in the proper clinical context, not simply episodic symptoms.
A normal test between episodes does not permanently exclude asthma.
Chest radiography can assess alternatives but does not demonstrate variable airflow limitation.
questions.explanation: The diagnosis combines a characteristic variable symptom pattern with objective evidence of variable expiratory airflow limitation.

questions.question: An adolescent with asthma is exhausted, speaks one word at a time, has oxygen saturation 88%, and now has minimal wheeze with very poor air movement. What is the safest interpretation?
choices: A quiet or silent chest can indicate critically reduced airflow and requires emergency escalation
Less wheeze proves the exacerbation has resolved
The findings support routine follow-up after an oral antihistamine
Low oxygen saturation is expected and does not alter urgency
rationales: Severe obstruction may produce too little airflow to generate wheeze; exhaustion and hypoxemia are life-threatening signs.
Decreasing wheeze with worsening air movement is ominous rather than reassuring.
Antihistamine does not treat severe lower-airway obstruction.
Hypoxemia and inability to speak normally materially increase urgency.
questions.explanation: Sound intensity depends on airflow. In severe asthma, a quieter chest can represent deterioration rather than improvement.

questions.question: An adult reports using only a short-acting bronchodilator several times each week for asthma symptoms. Which management concept best reflects current strategy guidance?
choices: Reassess control, technique, adherence, triggers, and ensure an inhaled-corticosteroid–containing treatment strategy
Continue bronchodilator-only treatment indefinitely because it eliminates airway inflammation
Add an antibiotic to prevent all future exacerbations
Stop all reliever access once symptoms improve for one day
rationales: Frequent symptoms warrant assessment and an ICS-containing strategy to address inflammatory risk, tailored to current guidance and the patient.
A short-acting bronchodilator relieves bronchoconstriction but does not treat underlying airway inflammation.
Routine antibiotics do not prevent asthma exacerbations.
Patients need an appropriate reliever and action plan; abrupt removal is unsafe.
questions.explanation: Advanced asthma care separates rapid symptom relief from reduction of future inflammatory exacerbation risk.

questions.question: A long-term smoker has progressive exertional dyspnea. Which finding is required to confirm persistent airflow obstruction consistent with COPD in the appropriate context?
choices: Post-bronchodilator spirometry showing a persistently reduced FEV1/FVC ratio
A normal chest radiograph
One episode of wheezing during a viral infection
Resting oxygen saturation below 90% in every case
rationales: COPD diagnosis requires spirometric confirmation of persistent post-bronchodilator airflow obstruction.
Chest radiographs may be normal and do not confirm airflow obstruction.
Transient wheeze is nonspecific.
Many patients with COPD have normal resting oxygen saturation, especially earlier in disease.
questions.explanation: Symptoms and exposure establish suspicion; post-bronchodilator spirometry confirms persistent obstruction.

questions.question: A patient with emphysema has hyperinflation and a reduced diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide. Which structural change best explains the low diffusion measurement?
choices: Destruction of alveolar walls reduces gas-exchange surface area and pulmonary capillary bed
Bronchial smooth-muscle hypertrophy increases alveolar surface area
Pleural thickening increases pulmonary capillary recruitment
Mucus hypersecretion raises hemoglobin concentration
rationales: Emphysematous destruction removes alveolar septa and adjacent capillaries, reducing diffusion area.
Airway smooth-muscle changes do not restore lost alveolar surface.
Pleural disease can restrict expansion but does not increase exchange surface.
Mucus does not increase hemoglobin or diffusion capacity.
questions.explanation: A reduced DLCO can help distinguish parenchymal destruction from some airway-predominant causes of obstruction.

questions.question: A patient with lobar pneumonia is hypoxemic because affected alveoli are perfused but filled with inflammatory material and poorly ventilated. Which gas-exchange abnormality predominates?
choices: Low V/Q approaching intrapulmonary shunt
High V/Q dead-space ventilation from absent perfusion
Pure hypoventilation with a normal A–a oxygen gradient
Increased diffusion area from alveolar consolidation
rationales: Blood passes poorly ventilated units, creating low V/Q and, when ventilation is absent, shunt physiology.
High V/Q describes ventilation without adequate perfusion, as in embolic obstruction.
Focal alveolar filling widens the A–a gradient rather than causing isolated uniform hypoventilation.
Consolidation impairs rather than increases effective gas exchange.
questions.explanation: Identifying whether ventilation or perfusion is missing predicts the physiology and helps interpret oxygen response.

questions.question: A patient receiving excessive sedative medication has slow shallow breathing, elevated PaCO2, and hypoxemia with no primary lung disease. Which mechanism best fits?
choices: Alveolar hypoventilation lowers alveolar oxygen while retaining carbon dioxide
Pulmonary embolism creates high-V/Q units with obligatory low PaCO2 only
Diffusion capacity rises because respiratory rate is low
An anatomic shunt causes isolated hyperventilation
rationales: Reduced alveolar ventilation directly raises PaCO2 and lowers alveolar and arterial oxygen.
Pulmonary embolism is not suggested by the medication exposure and global hypoventilation pattern.
A slow respiratory rate does not improve diffusion capacity.
A shunt does not explain sedative-induced hypoventilation and hypercapnia.
questions.explanation: Hypercapnia points toward inadequate effective ventilation unless CO2 production is extraordinarily high.

questions.question: A patient with diabetic ketoacidosis has deep, rapid respirations and PaCO2 lower than expected for normal physiology. What is the best interpretation?
choices: Respiratory compensation is increasing CO2 elimination to reduce the fall in pH
Primary respiratory acidosis is causing bicarbonate generation
The breathing pattern proves the metabolic acidosis is fully corrected
Hypoventilation is retaining CO2 to normalize pH
rationales: Kussmaul respirations lower PaCO2 as compensation for metabolic acidosis.
The primary disorder is metabolic acidosis, not respiratory acidosis.
Compensation limits pH change but does not correct the underlying ketoacid production.
Hypoventilation would raise CO2 and worsen acidemia.
questions.explanation: Compensation should be appropriate for the primary disorder; an unexpectedly high or low PaCO2 can reveal an additional respiratory disturbance.

questions.question: During fever and metabolic acidosis, how does the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve shift, and what is the physiologic effect?
choices: Right shift, facilitating oxygen unloading to tissues at a given PaO2
Left shift, facilitating oxygen unloading to tissues
Right shift, preventing oxygen release from hemoglobin
No shift because pH and temperature do not affect hemoglobin affinity
rationales: Higher temperature and lower pH reduce hemoglobin affinity, shifting the curve right and promoting tissue unloading.
A left shift increases affinity and impairs unloading at a given oxygen tension.
A right shift promotes rather than prevents release.
The Bohr effect describes the influence of pH and CO2 on affinity.
questions.explanation: A PaO2 value and hemoglobin saturation do not fully describe tissue unloading; affinity changes with the metabolic environment.

questions.question: After smoke exposure in an enclosed space, a patient has headache, confusion, and a pulse oximeter reading of 99%. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
choices: Standard pulse oximetry may falsely reassure in carbon monoxide exposure; obtain urgent evaluation with appropriate co-oximetry
The normal reading excludes clinically important carbon monoxide poisoning
Supplemental oxygen is contraindicated until carboxyhemoglobin is zero
Carbon monoxide causes only low V/Q mismatch visible on routine pulse oximetry
rationales: Conventional pulse oximeters cannot reliably distinguish oxyhemoglobin from carboxyhemoglobin, so exposure and symptoms require urgent specific assessment.
A normal displayed saturation does not exclude carboxyhemoglobinemia.
High-concentration oxygen is commonly used during emergency evaluation; treatment should not wait for a zero level.
The primary problem is abnormal hemoglobin binding and impaired oxygen delivery, not merely low V/Q.
questions.explanation: A monitor can be technically normal yet physiologically misleading when the measurement method cannot distinguish abnormal hemoglobin species.
